rationale: B wins because it finds the missing protagonist: the brand. “Brands get paid on day one. Who carries the 60-day float?” opens a real reporting lane A mostly ignores, while A’s “A wholesale marketplace becomes a bank: Faire's bet on embedded credit” is another lap around the same lender-risk track. A is competent; B is the set a founder can actually triage into separate fintech, retail, brand-side, and strategy pitches.
gaps_in_A: “A wholesale marketplace becomes a bank” overstates the facts. Faire is underwriting financing, but the update does not prove it is a bank or that the whole risk sits on its own balance sheet.

“underwriting directly off its own order-history data rather than routing through a named bank or BNPL partner” smuggles in a negative fact. No partner was disclosed; that is not the same as proving no partner exists.

The set circles the same story three times: “quietly becomes a lender,” “becomes a bank,” and “Someone is still paying for the risk.” Those can be sharpened, but they are not three fully separate pitches.
“cash flow, not demand” is a useful line, but it goes past the source. The update says cash flow is the top barrier to ordering; it does not prove demand is not a barrier.
gaps_in_B: “rather than a bank score” is not in the update. Order history is disclosed as an underwriting input; the absence of traditional credit scoring is not disclosed.
“Independent shops say cash flow, not demand” has the same overreach problem as A. Good angle, loose wording.

“The story is one shop owner and the order they didn't place” is a reporting assignment, not a fact. B mostly handles this by asking for proof, but the line still invents a little scene it has not earned.
